http://www.bgnes.com/weather/japanese-sh.text: Japanese shrimp that escaped from fish farms, where they had been used as fish feed, have multiplied rapidly in the Danube and Lake Razelm in the southern part of the Danube Delta over the past five years. They are already displacing crayfish, while biologists fear that the species could also pose a threat to pike, zander and perch. Meanwhile, the shrimp have become a popular dish in local restaurants, Romanian outlet Observator reported. At first glance, they may look like ordinary shrimp. However, they live not in the sea but in Romania’s fresh waters. Originally brought from Asia, they have spread into Lake Razelm and are becoming increasingly popular. In the town of Sarichioi, a 100-gram serving costs about $4.40. Restaurants in the Danube Delta have already begun adding the freshwater shrimp to their menus. The new population began appearing in crayfish traps along the Danube five years ago. The shrimp reproduce particularly rapidly during periods of hot weather. “This shrimp comes from Japan. It arrived at fish farms on the Dnieper and migrated from there through the delta, upstream along the Danube and into nearby lakes connected to the river,” said Dr Adrian Bîlbă. Fisherman Grigore Fârșă said the shoreline was “simply overflowing with these shrimp.” “They do not stay in deep water. The crayfish have disappeared — there are practically none left. When the water cools, the crayfish return and the shrimp disappear,” he added. Biologists fear that the new inhabitants of Lake Razelm could feed on the eggs of native fish and displace local species. “Studies are currently under way to determine their potential impact on native species. Any species that arrives here and reproduces in relatively large numbers is considered invasive,” said Aurel Năstase, a biologist at the Danube Delta National Institute for Research and Development. Sarichioi Mayor Vitali-Cristian Finoghen described the situation as “a small war that the shrimp are waging against other species.” “We hope they will adapt to this area so that we can make use of both our fish and these shrimp, as they are becoming something of a local speciality,” he said. | BGNES
